content.text: An LLM doesn't search a store of answers. It computes a probability for every possible next token, picks one, appends it and repeats. Its knowledge lives spread across its parameters, not in rows you can read or fix, which is why it can be fluent, confident and wrong at the same time.

A customer asks your support assistant about refunds. It answers, politely and confidently, that refunds are accepted within 60 days. Your policy says 30, and the number 60 appears nowhere in your docs. The product manager files a ticket: "Find the wrong entry in the model and correct it." The engineer who picks it up comes back empty-handed, because there is no entry. The model didn't retrieve "60 days" from anywhere. It generated it, one token at a time.
The common misconception
Many developers picture an LLM as a giant database of facts: your question goes in, the model searches its store, and the best-matching entry comes back. The picture is reasonable:

items.text: The interface looks like a search box. You type a question, you get an answer.
For well-known facts, answers are correct and stable. Ask for the capital of France ten times and you get Paris ten times, which is exactly how a lookup behaves.
"Trained on a huge amount of text" sounds like "keeps a copy of that text inside".
Some assistants really do search: with a web search tool, the app fetches pages before the model answers, which blurs the line.

content.text: It's a half-truth. The model does carry a lot of knowledge from training: Roberts, Raffel and Shazeer showed that language models can answer questions with no documents at hand, storing and retrieving knowledge
implicitly
in their parameters. But implicitly is the key word. There is no table, no index and no matching step.
What actually happens
Google's Machine Learning Crash Course defines a language model as one that estimates the probability of a
token
or sequence of tokens occurring within a longer sequence. A
large language model
does the same with a very large number of parameters: GPT-3, for example, has 175 billion. Generating an answer is a loop around that single prediction.
Your prompt is cut into tokens: whole words, pieces of words or single characters. The model never sees raw text.
The network reads every token in the context and outputs a probability for each token in its vocabulary. Not one answer: a whole distribution of candidates.
A sampling step chooses a token: the most likely one, or a random pick among the likely ones.
The chosen token joins the context and the whole prediction runs again with it, until the model signals that the answer is complete or a length limit is reached.
Where the facts actually live

Training adjusts the parameters so the model gets better at predicting the next token across a huge amount of text. To predict "The capital of France is ___" well, it has to absorb that "Paris" goes there. That knowledge doesn't land in a row labeled France. It's spread across many parameters that also encode grammar, style and countless other facts.

Three consequences follow. You can't list, edit or delete one fact the way you'd update a row. There is no "not found": every question produces a distribution, and something always has the highest probability. And the right answer is only as likely as training made it.

Declining to answer is learned behavior, not a failed lookup. Anthropic's interpretability team found that Claude's default circuit says it can't answer, and a "known entity" signal switches that default off for names it recognizes. When that signal misfires on a name it recognizes but knows little about, the model produces a plausible, untrue answer.
"Just autocomplete" is the opposite mistake

Google's course calls LLMs essentially autocomplete mechanisms. That's accurate about the output, one token at a time, but it doesn't mean the computation behind each token is shallow. When Anthropic traced Claude answering "the capital of the state containing Dallas", they saw it first represent "Dallas is in Texas", then "the capital of Texas is Austin". When they swapped the Texas concept for California, the answer became Sacramento. Writing a rhyming couplet, Claude picked the rhyme word before it wrote the line that ends on it.
So an LLM is neither a database nor a parrot. It produces text one token at a time, and each step can combine facts and plan ahead.
See the loop in a toy model
This script builds the oldest kind of language model, an n-gram model: it counts which word follows each run of
n
words in a tiny corpus. Real LLMs replace the count table with a Transformer of billions of parameters and a far longer context, but the generation loop is the same.

blocks.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

corpus = """the capital of france is paris . the capital of egypt is cairo .
the language of egypt is arabic . the language of france is french .""".split()

def train(n):  # "training": count which token follows every run of n tokens
    table = defaultdict(Counter)
    for i in range(len(corpus) - n):
        table[tuple(corpus[i:i + n])][corpus[i + n]] += 1
    return table

def generate(prompt, n):
    table, tokens = train(n), prompt.split()
    while tokens[-1] != ".":
        counts = table[tuple(tokens[-n:])]  # context = the last n tokens
        probs = {tok: c / sum(counts.values()) for tok, c in counts.items()}
        tokens.append(max(probs, key=probs.get))  # greedy: most likely token
    return " ".join(tokens)

print(train(1)[("is",)])  # 4 candidates, 1 count each: 25% each
print(generate("the capital of egypt is", n=1))
print(generate("the capital of atlantis is", n=1))
print(generate("the capital of egypt is", n=4))

content.text: With one token of context, all the model sees after "is" is four equally likely words, so it picks the first one and says the capital of Egypt is Paris. Atlantis doesn't exist, yet it gets Paris too: nothing comes back "not found", because nothing is searched. With four tokens of context, the same counts give "cairo". The knowledge was there all along; what changed is how much context the prediction used.

rows.text: The model searches a store of facts
It computes a probability for every possible next token
Each answer is a saved entry
Each answer is generated token by token, fresh every time
Some token always wins; saying "I don't know" is learned and can misfire
A wrong fact can be fixed in place
Knowledge is spread across parameters; change the context or retrain
A confident tone means it found the answer
Right and wrong answers come out of the same process

blocks.title: Need a lookup? Do the lookup yourself

content.text: Fetch the record from your database or docs and put it in the prompt, then ask the model to answer from that text. The 60-day bug turns into a data problem you can actually fix in one place.

The confident tone of a wrong answer comes from the same prediction loop as a right one, so it carries no signal of accuracy. Prices, policies, versions and IDs generated without your data in the prompt are guesses that read like facts. Don't show them to users unchecked.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Ground factual answers in your own data

content.text: For anything that must be right, such as policies, prices or account details, retrieve it from your system and include it in the prompt.

items.title: Fix the context, not the model

content.text: When the model states a wrong fact, read what was in its prompt first. Missing or ambiguous context is the usual cause, and the fix takes minutes. Retraining is slow and still won't give you a row to edit.

items.title: Test with many prompts, not one

content.text: Answers are generated, so a rephrased question or a second run can change them. Evaluate on a set of realistic variations before trusting a feature.
Numbers, dates, IDs and URLs in model output can be compared against your source of truth before they reach a user.
Key takeaways

items.text: An LLM doesn't search stored answers: it predicts a probability for every possible next token and generates text one token at a time.
Its knowledge lives implicitly in its parameters, so there's no record to read, edit or come back "not found".
A wrong answer comes out of the same process as a right one, so fluency isn't evidence.
"Just autocomplete" undersells it: inside, a model can chain facts and plan ahead.
When facts must be right, put them in the context and check the output.
